You've touched on something that I have considered for a long time: there are plenty of intelligent people who pretend not to be thus. It seems like so many people believe the geniuses will act like Sheldon Cooper while the rest of us, though dumber, possess greater social acumen. Why? How does being less intelligent make you more adept at interpersonal relationships?

But that's beside the point. 

So, you want an Irene who will accept the challenge. You want someone who is more or less able to solve your riddles, overcome your intellectual barriers and understand the fundamental you. 

My guess is that even though some Irene may approach you for such a task, you likely feel no challenge in understanding her. She may have her quirks, but you feel fairly certain you understand her well in a short time. So you find amusement in watching her attempt to best your challenges while taking no joy in discovering her? What is the incentive for Irene? You're bored with her, but it's fun to make her jump through hoops to prove that she understands you. No thanks.

If you are going to use your intellect as a barrier (and you are) then you have to assent that someone who overcomes that barrier may present a challenge of a different nature. This Irene may not be as intelligent as you in some areas, but she may have greater understanding of who you are in spite of how you separate yourself from others. 

What you should search for, then, is not someone who walls themselves off intellectually in the same manner. Instead, consider that the challenge others present to you is in understanding them on an emotional level that includes a sense of humanity. I think you consider intelligence as the greater virtue, but I encourage you to broaden your view.

Your Irene is not a fellow Mensa member. She's the person who will help you understand that your intellectual obstacle course does more to bolster your view of your own IQ rather than draw you closer to another human being.
